extractions.description: This paper examines the shortcomings of the standard training protocol for emergent multi-agent communication in populations, specifically in sender-receiver Lewis games. The authors highlight the issue of co-adaptation between interacting sender and receiver, which diminishes the benefits of having larger populations. They propose a new training protocol, called partitioning, to isolate sender-receiver pairs and limit co-adaptation. The results show improved communication with new agents and more compositional languages in larger populations.

sustainable_development_is_central.quote: Despite evidence from sociolinguistics that larger groups of speakers tend to develop more structured languages, the use of populations has failed to yield significant benefits in emergent multi-agent communication.

primary_category.quote: In this paper, we call into question the way such populations are trained. By studying a simple referential game, we evaluate populations on two desirable features observed in natural language.

secondary_sub_categories.quote: Our hypothesis is that, counter to what is customary in the emergent communication literature, tying senders and receivers is key in surfacing useful population-level dynamics in multi-agent communication.

applications.justification: The paper presents a new training protocol to improve communication and language compositionality among artificial agents, which could be applied to various tasks including simulations.
applications.quote: Informed by this analysis, we propose an alternative training protocol based on “partitioning” agents. Partitioning isolates sender-receiver pairs, limits co-adaptation, and results in a new global optimization objective.
